question: The 2025 Lancet Commission report on adolescent health and wellbeing accurately reflects the challenges faced by adolescents across the world: — an increased incidence of mental health disorders among adolescents, — increasing rates of obesity, — limited access to health services and psychosocial support, — cyber bullying, disinformation and inequalities in reproductive health, — insufficient protection against violence, inside and outside the home.

It is worth noting that although adolescents account for 24 % of the world’s population, they receive only 2.4 % of the relevant funding for health and development policy. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Is there a plan to strengthen funding tools (EU4Health, ESF+, Horizon Europe) for national or cross-border programmes targeting mental health, obesity prevention and reproductive education for adolescents?
What is the Commission’s strategy for protecting adolescents from commercial exploitation in digital media (food advertising, disinformation, screen addiction)?
How can the prevention of physical and psychological abuse against adolescents be strengthened?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.10.2025) The Commission supports Member States on preventive health through the Healthier Together initiative1. The Communication on a comprehensive approach to mental health2 provides actions to improve youth’s mental health. The Joint Action PERCH3 addresses reproductive health by aiming to boost HPV vaccination.

Over EUR 260 million were invested4,5 on youth mental health research and adolescent health6. Funding opportunities will be provided under Horizon Europe7. The European Social Fund Plus8 contributes to improving access to healthcare for disadvantaged groups. Moreover, the Commission is developing an ambitious Cardiovascular Health Plan to address the triangle of obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.

Preparatory work for an EU-wide inquiry9 on the broad impact of social media and excessive screentime on mental health and wellbeing is ongoing. The Digital Services Act10 sets strict rules to protect minors online, supported by Commission guidelines11 which enshrine safety and privacy by design.

A blueprint for age verification online12 was launched for +18 users to easily and in full respect of privacy access age restricted content. The upcoming EU action plan against cyberbullying will focus on minors and vulnerable youth. The Commission will propose a Digital Fairness Act to strengthen consumer protection in the digital space, focusing on children.

The Commission also recommends Member States to implement integrated child protection systems13. The Commission will update the Guidelines for teachers to foster digital literacy and tackle disinformation14 to address i.e., social media platforms. The upcoming 2030 Roadmap on the future of digital education and skills15, will focus on youth digital literacy and well-being. 1 https://health.ec.europa.
